# `silk/f32`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

IEEE binary32 values with deterministic representation, classification, and math operations.

## When to use
Use `f32` when binary32 storage, interchange, or bandwidth is part of the contract. Use `f64`
for general floating-point work and unconstrained literals; it preserves substantially more
precision and is Silk's default floating type.

## Details
Basic arithmetic rounds to nearest with ties to even and never enables implicit fast-math
assumptions. Division by zero and overflow produce IEEE infinities or NaNs rather than integer-
style traps. Ordinary ordered comparisons return false for NaN and treat both zeros as equal;
[`totalOrder`](#declaration-) distinguishes every encoding when deterministic ordering is required.

[`toBits`](#declaration-) and [`fromBits`](#declaration-) expose the exact binary32 representation, including signed zero and
NaN payloads. The source-defined rounding, extrema, sign, and square-root helpers canonicalize
NaN results so native and WebAssembly execution agree on their bits.

## Gotchas
Converting to an integer discards the fractional part and traps for NaN, infinity, or a value
outside the destination range. The `checkedTo*` counterparts return `None` on exactly those
inputs instead of trapping. Converting a large integer to f32 can round it.

## Examples
### Inspect a binary32 boundary by its bits
```silk
import silk.f32

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let rounded = f32.round(-0.25)
  if f32.toBits(rounded) != f32.toBits(-0.0) {
    return 1
  }
  if !f32.isNaN(f32.sqrt(-1.0)) {
    return 2
  }
  return 42
}
```

Import as `f32` with `import silk.f32`.

## `INFINITY`

```silk
pub const INFINITY: f32
```

Positive infinity with the binary32 bit pattern `0x7F800000`.

### Details

No source literal spells infinity directly. This initializer deliberately exceeds [`MAX`](#declaration-), and
decimal-to-binary32 rounding produces the infinity encoding.

## `remainder`

```silk
pub fn remainder(left: f32, right: f32) -> f32
```

Returns `left - trunc(left / right) * right`. A zero `right`, infinite `left`, or NaN operand
produces NaN; it does not trap.

## `totalOrder`

```silk
pub fn totalOrder(left: f32, right: f32) -> bool
```

Reports whether `left` precedes or equals `right` in the IEEE total order.

### When to use

Use this function for deterministic ordering that includes NaNs and distinguishes signed zero.

### Details

Unlike ordinary comparison, this order distinguishes negative and positive zero and provides a
deterministic position for NaN encodings.

<a id="declaration-"></a>

## `sqrt`

```silk
pub fn sqrt(value: f32) -> f32
```

Computes the correctly rounded square root and preserves either signed zero.

### Details

IEEE requires square root to be correctly rounded, so its native and WebAssembly instructions
have one admissible numeric result.

### Gotchas

NaN and negative nonzero inputs return the canonical quiet NaN. Negative zero is not treated as
negative and returns unchanged.

<a id="declaration-"></a>

## `trunc`

```silk
pub fn trunc(value: f32) -> f32
```

Rounds toward zero while preserving the sign of a zero result.

### Details

A value in `(-1.0, -0.0]` becomes negative zero. A NaN becomes the canonical quiet NaN, while
either infinity is already integral and returns unchanged.

<a id="declaration-"></a>

## `round`

```silk
pub fn round(value: f32) -> f32
```

Rounds to the nearest integral f32, with a half rounded away from zero.

### Details

This differs from the ties-to-even policy used by basic arithmetic. A zero result keeps its
input sign, and a NaN becomes the canonical quiet NaN.

<a id="declaration-"></a>

<a id="declaration-"></a>

## `checkedToU8`

```silk
pub fn checkedToU8(value: f32) -> Option<u8>
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `u8`, or returns `None` when the truncated result is out of
range.

### When to use

Use this function when a NaN, an infinity, or an out-of-range magnitude is input data rather
than a program error. [`toU8`](#declaration-) traps on exactly the inputs this function reports as `None`.

### Details

The fraction is discarded first, so the range test applies to the truncated value: a magnitude
below one is in range and yields zero. The truncated value is accepted when it is at least zero
and below `2^8`. Both bounds are powers of two and so are exact in binary32; a bound converted
from `u8.MAX` would round outward and wrongly admit an overflowing value.

### Gotchas

NaN and either infinity return `None`. A value in `(-1.0, -0.0]` truncates to negative zero and
converts to `0`, so its sign is discarded rather than rejected.

<a id="declaration-"></a>

## `checkedToUsize`

```silk
pub fn checkedToUsize(value: f32) -> Option<usize>
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `usize`, or returns `None` when the truncated result is out of
range.

### When to use

Use this function when a NaN, an infinity, or an out-of-range magnitude is input data rather
than a program error. [`toUsize`](#declaration-) traps on exactly the inputs this function reports as `None`.

### Details

The fraction is discarded first, so the range test applies to the truncated value: a magnitude
below one is in range and yields zero. `usize` follows the selected target's pointer width, so
the bounds follow it too. The truncated value is accepted when it is at least zero and below
`2^32` on a 32-bit target or `2^64` on a 64-bit one.

Every bound is a power of two and so is exact in binary32. A bound converted from `usize.MAX`
would round outward and wrongly admit an overflowing value, and a bound fixed at 64-bit width
would admit values that trap on a 32-bit target.

### Gotchas

NaN and either infinity return `None`. A value in `(-1.0, -0.0]` truncates to negative zero and
converts to `0`, so its sign is discarded rather than rejected.

<a id="declaration-"></a>
